title: Unlettered apostles and the power of their preaching
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα δ᾿ ἐπεὶ μηδὲ τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐπιστάμενος δέκα εἶπεν ἢ ἕνδεκά τινας ἐξαρτησάμενον τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἑαυτῷ ἐπιῤῥήτους ἀνθρώπους, τελώνας καὶ ναύτας τοὺς πονηροτάτους, μετὰ τούτων τῇδε κἀκεῖσε αὐτὸν ἀποδεδρακέναι, αἰσχρῶς καὶ γλίσχρως τροφὰς συνάγοντα, φέρε καὶ περὶ τούτων κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν διαλάβωμεν. φανερὸν δέ ἐστι τοῖς ἐντυγχάνουσιν εὐαγγελικοῖς λόγοις, οὓς οὐδ᾿ ἀνεγνωκέναι ὁ Κέλσος φαίνεται, ὅτι δώδεκα ἀποστόλους ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐπελέξατο, τελώνην μὲν τὸν Ματθαῖον, οὓς δ᾿ εἶπε συγκεχυμένως ναύτας τάχα τὸν Ἰάκωβον καὶ τὸν Ἰωάννην φησὶν, ἐπεὶ καταλιπόντες τὸ πλοῖον καὶ „τὸν πατέρα αὐτῶν Ζεβεδαῖον“ ἠκολούθησαν τῷ Ἰησοῦ. τὸν γὰρ Πέτρον καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ Ἀνδρέαν, ἀμφιβλήστρῳ χρωμένους διὰ τὰς ἀναγκαίας τροφὰς, οὐκ ἐν ναύταις ἀλλ᾿, ὡς ἀνέγραψεν ἡ γραφὴ, ἐν ἁλιεῦσιν ἀριθμητέον. ἔστω δὲ καὶ ὁ Λευὴς τελώνης ἀκολουθήσας τῷ Ἰησοῦ· ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τῶν ἀποστόλων αὐτοῦ ἦν εἰ μὴ κατά τινα τῶν ἀντιγράφων τοῦ κατὰ Μάρκον εὐαγγελίου. τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν οὐ μεμαθήκαμεν τὰ ἔργα, ὅθεν πρὸ τῆς μαθητείας τοῦ Ἰησοῦ περιεποίουν ἑαυτοῖς τὰς τροφάς. φημὶ οὖν καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα ὅτι τοῖς δυναμένοις φρονίμως καὶ εὐγνωμόνως ἐξετάζειν τὰ περὶ τοὺς ἀποστόλους τοῦ Ἰησοῦ φαίνεται ὅτι δυνάμει θείᾳ ἐδίδασκον οὗτοι τὸν χριστιανισμὸν καὶ ἐπετύγχανον ὑπάγοντες ἀνθρώπους τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θεοῦ. οὐ γὰρ ἡ εἰς τὸ λέγειν δύναμις καὶ τάξις ἀπαγγελίας κατὰ τὰς Ἑλλήνων διαλεκτικὰς ἢ ῥητορικὰς τέχνας ἦν ἐν αὐτοῖς ὑπαγομένη τοὺς ἀκούοντας. δοκεῖ δέ μοι ὅτι σοφοὺς μέν τινας ὡς πρὸς τὴν τῶν πολλῶν ὑπόληψιν καὶ ἱκανοὺς πρὸς τὸ νοεῖν ἀρεσκόντως πλήθεσι καὶ λέγειν ἐπιλεξάμενος καὶ χρησάμενος αὐτοῖς διακόνοις τῆς διδασκαλίας ὁ Ἰησοῦς εὐλογώτατ᾿ ἂν ὑπενοήθη ὁμοίᾳ φιλοσόφοις κεκηρύχθαι ἀγωγῇ, αἱρέσεώς τινος προϊσταμένοις· καὶ οὐκέτ᾿ ἂν ἡ περὶ τοῦ θεῖον εἶναι τον λόγον ἐπαγγελία ἀνεφαίνετο, ἅτε τοῦ λόγου ὄντος καὶ τοῦ κηρύγματος ἐν πειθοῖς τῆς ἐν φράσει καὶ συνθέσει τῶν λέξεων σοφίας· καὶ ἦν ἂν „ἡ πίστις“ ὁμοίως τῇ τῶν τοῦ κόσμου φιλοσόφων περὶ τῶν δογμάτων πίστει „ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων“ καὶ οὐκ „ἐν δυνάμει θεοῦ“· νυνὶ δὲ τίς βλέπων ἁλιεῖς καὶ τελώνας μηδὲ τὰ πρῶτα γράμματα μεμαθηκότας (ὡς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἀναγράφει περὶ αὐτῶν καὶ ὁ Κέλσος κατὰ ταῦτα πεπίστευκεν αὐτοῖς, ἀληθεύουσι περὶ τῆς ἰδιωτείας αὐτῶν), τεθαῤῥηκότως οὐ μόνον Ἰουδαίοις ὁμιλοῦντας περὶ τῆς εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν πίστεως ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τοῖς λοιποῖς ἔθνεσι κηρύσσοντας αὐτὸν καὶ ἀνύοντας, οὐκ ἂν ζητήσαι, πόθεν ἦν αὐτοῖς δύναμις πειστική; οὐ γὰρ ἡ νενομισμένη τοῖς πολλοῖς. καὶ τίς οὐκ ἂν λέγοι ὅτι τὸ „δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου, καὶ ποιήσω ὑμᾶς ἁλιεῖς ἀνθρώπων“ δυνάμει τινὶ θείᾳ ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ ἐπλήρωσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς; ἥντινα καὶ ὁ Παῦλος παριστὰς, ὡς καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρήκαμεν, φησί· „καὶ ὁ λόγος μου καὶ τὸ κήρυγμά μου οὐκ ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις ἀλλ᾿ ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, ἵν᾿ ἡ πίστις ἡμῶν μὴ ᾖ ἐν σοφίᾳ ἁνθρώπων ἀλλ᾿ ἐν δυνάμει θεοῦ.“ κατὰ γὰρ τὰ εἰρημένα ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, προγνωστικῶς ἀπαγγέλλουσι περὶ τῆς κηρύξεως τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, „κύριος ἔδωκε ῥῆμα τοῖς εὐαγγελιζομένοις δυνάμει πολλῇ, ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν δυνάμεων τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ,“ ἵνα καὶ ἡ λέγουσα προφητεία· „ἕως τάχους δραμεῖται ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ“ πληρωθῇ. καὶ βλέπομέν γε ὅτι „εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ἐξῆλθεν ὁ“ τῶν ἀποστόλων Ἰησοῦ „φθόγγος, καὶ εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς οἰκουμένης τὰ ῥήματα αὐτῶν.“ διὰ τοῦτο δυνάμεως μὲν πληροῦνται οἱ λόγου τοῦ μετὰ δυνάμεως ἀπαγγελλομένου ἀκούοντες, ἣν ἐπιδείκνυνται τῇ τε διαθέσει καὶ τῷ βίῳ καὶ τῷ ἕως θανάτου ἀγωνίζεσθαι περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας· διάκενοι δέ τινες εἰσὶ, κἂν ἐπαγγέλλωνται πιστεύειν τῷ θεῷ διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, οἱ μὴ δύναμιν θείαν ἔχοντες προσάγεσθαι δοκοῦντες τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θεοῦ. εἰ καὶ ἀνωτέρω δ᾿ ἐμνήσθην εὐαγγελικοῦ ῥητοῦ ὑπὸ τοῦ σωτῆρος εἰρημένου, οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ νῦν αὐτῷ κατὰ καιρὸν χρήσομαι, παριστὰς καὶ τὴν τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν περὶ τῆς τοῦ εὐαγγελίου κηρύξεως πρόγνωσιν θειότατα δηλουμένην καὶ τὴν τοῦ λόγου ἰσχὺν, χωρὶς διδασκάλων κρατοῦσαν τῶν πιστευόντων τῇ μετὰ δυνάμεως θείας πειθοῖ. φησὶ δὴ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· „ὁ μὲν θερισμὸς πολὺς, οἱ δὲ ἐργάται ὀλίγοι· δεήθητε οὖν τοῦ κυρίου τοῦ θερισμοῦ, ὅπως ἐκβάλῃ ἐργάτας εἰς τὸν θερισμὸν αὐτοῦ.“
pass_a_gloss: After these, since not even knowing the number of the apostles he said that Jesus, having attached (ἐξαρτησάμενον) to himself ten or eleven notorious (ἐπιρρήτους) men, tax collectors (τελώνας) and sailors (ναύτας) the most wicked (πονηροτάτους), with these ran away (ἀποδεδρακέναι) here and there, collecting food shamefully and meanly (αἰσχρῶς καὶ γλίσχρως), come, let us also treat (διαλάβωμεν) these as far as possible. It is clear to those reading (ἐντυγχάνουσιν) the gospel accounts (εὐαγγελικοῖς λόγοις), which Celsus appears not even to have read, that Jesus chose (ἐπελέξατο) twelve apostles, Matthew a tax collector, and those he called confusedly (συγκεχυμένως) sailors he perhaps (τάχα) means James and John, since leaving the boat and 'their father Zebedee' they followed Jesus. For Peter and his brother Andrew, using a casting net (ἀμφιβλήστρῳ) for necessary food, must be numbered not among sailors but, as the scripture (γραφή) recorded, among fishermen (ἁλιεῦσιν). Let Levi too be a tax collector who followed Jesus; but he was not of the number of his apostles except according to some of the copies (ἀντιγράφων) of the Gospel according to Mark. Of the rest we have not learned the works (ἔργα) by which before the discipleship (μαθητεία) of Jesus they provided food for themselves. I say then also to these that to those able to examine prudently (φρονίμως) and fair-mindedly (εὐγνωμόνως) the things about the apostles of Jesus it appears that by divine power (δυνάμει θείᾳ) these taught Christianity (χριστιανισμόν) and succeeded (ἐπετύγχανον) in bringing men under (ὑπάγοντες) the word (λόγῳ) of God. For not the power for speaking and order of delivery (τάξις ἀπαγγελίας) according to the dialectical or rhetorical arts (τέχνας) of the Greeks was in them bringing the hearers under. It seems to me that, having chosen some wise as to the opinion (ὑπόληψιν) of the many and competent to think and speak pleasingly to crowds, and using them as ministers (διακόνοις) of the teaching, Jesus would most reasonably have been suspected to have been proclaimed by a method (ἀγωγῇ) like philosophers heading some school (αἱρέσεως); and no longer would the promise/claim (ἐπαγγελία) about the word being divine appear, since the word and the preaching (κήρυγμα) would be in persuasions (πειθοῖς) of wisdom in phrasing (φράσει) and composition (συνθέσει) of words; and 'the faith (πίστις)' would be, like the faith of the philosophers of the world about doctrines (δογμάτων), 'in wisdom of men' and not 'in power of God'. But now who, seeing fishermen and tax collectors who had not learned even the first letters (as the gospel records about them, and Celsus on these has believed them, telling truth about their lack of learning (ἰδιωτείας)), boldly speaking not only to Jews about faith in Jesus but also preaching him among the other nations and accomplishing (ἀνύοντας), would not ask whence they had persuasive power (δύναμις πειστική)? For not the one customary among the many. And who would not say that the 'come after me, and I will make you fishers of men' Jesus fulfilled (ἐπλήρωσεν) by some divine power in his apostles? Which Paul too presenting, as we said above, says: 'and my word and my preaching not in persuasive words of human wisdom but in demonstration (ἀποδείξει) of spirit (πνεύματος) and power, that our faith may not be in wisdom of men but in power of God.' For according to what was said in the prophets, announcing foreknowingly (προγνωστικῶς) about the preaching of the gospel, 'the Lord gave a word (ῥῆμα) to those proclaiming good news with much power, the king of the powers of the beloved (ἀγαπητοῦ)', that also the prophecy saying 'his word will run until swiftness (ἕως τάχους)' might be fulfilled. And we see that 'into all the earth went out the sound (φθόγγος)' of the apostles of Jesus, 'and to the ends of the inhabited world (οἰκουμένης) their words'. Through this those hearing the word proclaimed with power are filled with power, which they display in disposition (διαθέσει) and life and struggling until death about the truth; but some are empty (διάκενοι), even if they profess to believe in God through Jesus, those not having divine power, seeming to be brought (προσάγεσθαι) to the word of God. Even if above I mentioned a gospel saying (ῥητοῦ) spoken by the Saviour, none the less now too I will use it in season, presenting both our Saviour's foreknowledge (πρόγνωσιν) about the preaching of the gospel shown most divinely and the strength (ἰσχύν) of the word, prevailing (κρατοῦσαν) without teachers over those believing by the persuasion (πειθοῖ) with divine power. Jesus says: 'the harvest is much, the workers few; pray then the Lord of the harvest that he cast out (ἐκβάλῃ) workers into his harvest.'
pass_b_english: After this, since Celsus, not even knowing the number of the apostles, said that Jesus “attached to himself ten or eleven notorious men, tax collectors and sailors of the worst sort, and with them ran away here and there, gathering his food in a shameful and beggarly way,” come, let us deal with these points too, as far as we can. It is plain to those who read the Gospel accounts, which Celsus seems not even to have read, that Jesus chose twelve apostles (Matthew 10:1–4), of whom Matthew was a tax collector (Matthew 10:3). By those whom he loosely called sailors he perhaps means James and John, since they left the boat and “their father Zebedee” and followed Jesus (Matthew 4:21–22). For Peter and his brother Andrew, who used a casting net to get the food they needed, must be counted not among sailors but, as Scripture recorded, among fishermen (Matthew 4:18). Granted that Levi too, a tax collector, followed Jesus (Mark 2:14); yet he was not of the number of his apostles, except in some copies of the Gospel according to Mark. Of the rest we have not learned the trades by which they earned their food before they became disciples of Jesus.

To this, then, I say that those who are able to examine the story of the apostles of Jesus with good sense and fairness can see that these men taught Christianity by divine power and succeeded in winning people over to the word of God. For what was in them and won over their hearers was not a power of speech or an ordered delivery shaped by the dialectical or rhetorical arts of the Greeks. It seems to me that if Jesus had chosen men who were wise in the opinion of the multitude and able to think and speak in a way that pleases crowds, and had used them as ministers of his teaching, he would with very good reason have been suspected of having been proclaimed by a method like that of philosophers who stand at the head of some school. Then the claim that the message is divine would no longer have shone out, since the message and the preaching would have rested on the persuasiveness of a wisdom that lies in the phrasing and arrangement of words (1 Corinthians 2:4); and “faith,” like the faith that the philosophers of the world have in their doctrines, would have been “in the wisdom of men” and not “in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:5).

But as it is, the Gospel records that these fishermen and tax collectors had not learned even their first letters (Acts 4:13), and on this point Celsus has believed them, as telling the truth about their lack of learning. Who, then, seeing such men speaking boldly not only to Jews about faith in Jesus but also preaching him among the other nations, and succeeding, would not ask where their power to persuade came from? For it was not the kind that most people are used to. And who would not say that Jesus fulfilled the words “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19) by some divine power in his apostles? Paul too sets this power before us, as we have also said above, when he says: “And my word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not be in the wisdom of men but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5). For, as was said in the prophets, who announced beforehand the preaching of the gospel, “The Lord gave a word to those who preach the good news with great power, the King of the powers of the beloved” (Psalm 68:11–12), so that the prophecy which says, “His word will run swiftly” (Psalm 147:15), might also be fulfilled. And indeed we see that the “sound” of the apostles of Jesus “has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19:4; Romans 10:18).

That is why those who hear the word proclaimed with power are filled with power, and they show it in their disposition, in their life, and in their struggle for the truth even to death. But some are empty, even though they profess to believe in God through Jesus: those who seem to be brought to the word of God without having divine power. Though I have already mentioned above a saying in the Gospel spoken by the Saviour, I will nonetheless use it again now, since the moment calls for it, to show both our Saviour's foreknowledge about the preaching of the gospel, made known in a most divine way, and the strength of the word, which without teachers prevails over those who believe, by a persuasion joined with divine power. Jesus says: “The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38).

choices.choice: Celsus's charge is given in indirect speech in the Greek (εἶπεν with infinitives); it is rendered as a quotation of his words in third person, as Origen frames it, and Origen repeats its key words in 1.63. 'Come, let us deal with these points' renders φέρε ... διαλάβωμεν. Peter and Andrew's casting net (ἀμφίβληστρον) is Matthew 4:18 (also Mark 1:16). On Levi: Mark 2:14 names 'Levi son of Alphaeus' as a tax collector; Origen's remark that Levi is counted among the apostles in some copies of Mark likely refers to a variant at Mark 3:18 (Western witnesses read Lebbaeus for Thaddaeus); this identification is probable, not certain, so it is not cited inline. 'As the Gospel records of them' (ὡς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἀναγράφει) points to the description of Peter and John as ἀγράμματοι καὶ ἰδιῶται, which stands in Acts 4:13, not in a Gospel; Origen's word εὐαγγέλιον is kept and the verse cited. 1 Corinthians 2:4-5 is quoted with ἡμῶν ('our faith') where the New Testament reads ὑμῶν ('your faith'); Origen's reading is translated. The 'above' cross-reference for Paul's words points to an earlier chapter of Book 1 (1 Corinthians 2:4 is cited near the start of the work), not pinpointed here. LXX Psalm numbering converted: LXX Psalm 67:12-13 = English Psalm 68:11-12 (quoted from the LXX, 'The Lord gave a word to those who preach good news with great power, the King of the powers of the beloved'; Origen has ἔδωκε, past, where most LXX copies read δώσει, future; translated as 'gave'; the LXX differs markedly from the Hebrew); LXX Psalm 147:4 = English Psalm 147:15 (ἕως τάχους δραμεῖται ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ); LXX Psalm 18:5 = English Psalm 19:4 (also quoted in Romans 10:18), with Origen inserting 'of the apostles of Jesus' in place of αὐτῶν, so the quotation marks are split around his insertion. 'Ask the Lord of the harvest to send out' renders δεήθητε ... ὅπως ἐκβάλῃ, the wording of Matthew 9:38 (compare Luke 10:2). The 'saying mentioned above' is this same harvest saying, cited earlier in Book 1; not pinpointed here. The parenthesis ὡς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ... ἰδιωτείας αὐτῶν is set as its own sentence before the question, to avoid nested brackets around the Acts citation; no words are added beyond the connective 'then' and 'such men'.
ὑπάγοντες ... τῷ λόγῳ: calque 'bringing people under the word' changed to 'winning people over to the word'
sentence on Greek rhetorical arts put into natural English order
added inline (1 Corinthians 2:4) for the clear allusion 'persuasiveness of a wisdom'; 'philosophers of this world' changed to 'of the world' (no τούτου)
nested parenthesis with (Acts 4:13) recast as a separate sentence before the question
οὐ γὰρ ἡ νενομισμένη: 'not the kind commonly supposed' changed to 'not the kind that most people are used to'
παριστάς: agency restored to Origen ('I will use it ... to show'), not 'It shows'; κρατοῦσαν rendered 'prevails over'
